answerKey.primaryProblem: Excessive saturated fat and simple carbohydrate intake with inadequate fruit/vegetable and fiber intake related to irregular shift-work meal pattern, reliance on convenience foods, and limited nutrition knowledge, as evidenced by LDL 195 mg/dL, HDL 30 mg/dL, triglycerides 180 mg/dL, total cholesterol 260 mg/dL, BMI 29.2, and waist circumference 43 inches.
differential: Primary (familial) hyperlipidemia given strong family history of early CAD - warrants consideration though diet/lifestyle factors are clearly contributory
Medication non-adherence as independent driver of poor lipid control (statin taken inconsistently)
Metabolic syndrome / insulin resistance component (elevated fasting glucose, HbA1c 5.8%, central adiposity, hypertension, low HDL, elevated triglycerides) amplifying cardiovascular risk
Secondary dyslipidemia contributors to rule out via PCP: hypothyroidism, excess alcohol intake (patient reports regular beer consumption which can raise triglycerides)
keyFindings: LDL 195 mg/dL and HDL 30 mg/dL indicate high atherogenic risk out of proportion to total cholesterol alone
Triglycerides 180 mg/dL and fasting glucose 110 mg/dL with HbA1c 5.8% show early insulin resistance pattern consistent with prediabetes
BMI 29.2 with waist circumference 43 inches indicates central adiposity, a modifiable CV risk factor
BP 148/92 mmHg confirms uncontrolled hypertension compounding risk despite reported consistent lisinopril use
Dietary pattern: skipped breakfast, heavy dinner, frequent fast food, minimal produce, regular soda, and nightly beer intake are the key modifiable nutrition-related behaviors
Statin adherence is inconsistent due to perceived dizziness; patient has not disclosed this to prescriber
Patient is in precontemplation for medication change but contemplation for dietary change - counseling should prioritize diet-focused goals first to build engagement
plan: Document findings using ADIME format with PES statement, e.g.: 'Excessive saturated fat and inadequate fiber intake related to irregular shift-work schedule and reliance on convenience/fast foods as evidenced by LDL 195 mg/dL, HDL 30 mg/dL, triglycerides 180 mg/dL, and waist circumference 43 inches.'
Negotiate 1-2 small, specific, achievable goals aligned with patient's stated motivations (grandkids, returning to full work) rather than a full diet overhaul
Introduce practical substitutions compatible with shift work: packable high-fiber snacks, swapping 1 soda/day for water or unsweetened beverage, adding one fruit or vegetable at each meal
Discuss sources of soluble fiber (oats, beans, fruit) and plant sterols to support LDL reduction alongside, not instead of, statin therapy
Address alcohol intake nonjudgmentally and its contribution to elevated triglycerides; explore readiness to reduce frequency/amount

Coordinate with PCP/pharmacy regarding reported statin-related dizziness and lisinopril-related cough rather than patient unilaterally stopping medication - encourage patient to report these symptoms rather than self-discontinue
Clarify misconceptions about cholesterol numbers and statin mechanism in plain language, using the 'ask-tell-ask' approach
Provide referral/follow-up plan: repeat lipid panel and HbA1c in 3 months, follow-up nutrition visit in 2-4 weeks to assess progress and barriers
Involve spouse in meal planning conversation if patient is open to it, leveraging existing support system
Discuss hydration goal and reducing sugar-sweetened beverage intake as a concrete first step
redFlags: Uncontrolled BP (148/92) in setting of newly diagnosed dyslipidemia and prediabetes raises near-term cardiovascular risk - warrants timely PCP follow-up, not just nutrition counseling alone
Unreported medication side effects (statin-associated dizziness, ACE-inhibitor cough) risking unsupervised discontinuation of cardioprotective medications
Strong family history of early coronary artery disease combined with current risk factor clustering (metabolic syndrome pattern) elevates urgency of risk-factor modification
Low HDL (30 mg/dL) is an independent CV risk factor often under-recognized by patients who focus only on total/LDL cholesterol
educationPoints: Explain LDL, HDL, and triglycerides in plain, practical terms (e.g., LDL as 'extra buildup' risk, HDL as 'the one you want higher') tailored to his health literacy level
Clarify that statin-associated muscle aches are a known but manageable side effect, and that abruptly stopping is riskier than reporting symptoms to the prescriber
Reinforce that dietary change and medication work together, not as alternatives, to lower cardiovascular risk
Normalize shift-work challenges and tailor recommendations to be realistic for his schedule (grab-and-go, batch prep on days off)
Use motivational interviewing: reflect his stated motivations (grandkids, staying on the job) to build intrinsic motivation for both diet and medication adherence
Emphasize that small, sustainable changes (one swap at a time) are more realistic than an all-or-nothing approach given his skepticism and busy schedule

cells: Lower LDL cholesterol / reduce CV risk

facts.chart: Patient referred by PCP for medical nutrition therapy for new dyslipidemia diagnosis
facts.says: My doctor said my cholesterol's high and sent me to talk to you. I don't really see what the big deal is, honestly.

facts.says: I'm an aircraft mechanic. Been doing it twenty years. Shifts can run ten, twelve hours sometimes.

facts.chart: 45-year-old male, married

facts.chart: Lives with spouse and young children
facts.says: Yeah, it's me, my wife, and our two kids at home.

facts.chart: Reports eating approximately 3 meals a day when directly asked, though recall reveals skipped breakfast

facts.says: Lunch is whatever's fastest - there's a burger place right by the hangar, I probably hit it four or five times a week.

facts.says: Dinner's the big meal. My wife cooks, or I'll throw something on the grill - burgers, sausage, whatever. We don't do a lot of vegetables, I'll be honest.

facts.chart: Low fruit and vegetable intake, cites cost and inconvenience
facts.says: Fruits and vegetables? Man, that stuff's expensive and it goes bad before you can eat it all. We just don't keep much of it around.

facts.chart: Drinks 2-3 cans of regular soda daily; minimal water intake
facts.says: I drink soda, probably two, three cans a day. Water's just... boring, I don't really think to grab it.

facts.says: I'll have a couple beers most nights after my shift, it helps me wind down. Weekends when I'm grilling it might be a few more.

facts.says: I'm on my feet at work but it's not like exercise. On my days off I'm honestly just tired, I don't do much.

facts.says: My sleep's all over the place with the shifts. Some nights I get five, six hours if I'm lucky.

facts.says: Sometimes after I take that cholesterol pill I feel kind of dizzy, lightheaded. I didn't tell the doctor, I just started skipping it some days.

facts.chart: Inconsistent atorvastatin adherence, misses several doses per week
facts.says: I'd say I probably miss it two, three times a week. If I'm not feeling right I just don't take it.

facts.chart: Persistent dry cough attributed to lisinopril, takes medication consistently despite this
facts.says: The blood pressure pill gives me this cough that won't quit, but I still take that one every day, that one scares me less.

facts.chart: Believes statins cause muscle pain and are generally harmful long-term
facts.says: Everybody at work says those statin pills mess up your muscles and your liver. I don't love putting that stuff in my body.

facts.chart: Limited understanding of cholesterol numbers; believes his levels are not concerning
facts.says: 260, 195, whatever - nobody's really explained what those numbers actually mean. I feel fine, so I figured it can't be that bad.

facts.chart: Perceives recommended dietary changes as too restrictive and expensive
facts.says: I don't want somebody telling me I gotta eat salad every day. That's not realistic with my schedule or my wallet.

facts.chart: Motivated by desire to stay healthy for grandchildren and avoid heart attack
facts.says: My dad had a heart attack at 52 and it scared the hell out of me. I want to be around to see my grandkids someday.

facts.chart: Motivated to return to/maintain full work shifts without fatigue
facts.says: I need to be able to work full shifts without feeling wiped out. That's non-negotiable, I've got a family to support.

facts.chart: Fears health problems could jeopardize his job
facts.says: If I can't keep up at work, that's a real problem for us financially. I can't afford to be out sick all the time.

facts.chart: Father had myocardial infarction at age 52; strong family history of early coronary artery disease
facts.says: My dad had his heart attack at 52. That's part of why this whole cholesterol thing worries me more than I let on.

facts.chart: History of severe migraines, not currently active, unrelated to current visit
facts.says: I used to get these awful migraines a few years back, knock-you-out kind. Haven't had one in a while though.

facts.chart: No prior cardiac events (no MI, no stents, no angina)

facts.chart: No known food or medication allergies

facts.chart: Spouse supportive of healthier eating but limited involvement in meal prep due to her own work schedule
facts.says: My wife's on board with eating healthier, she just works a lot too so it's not like she's got time to cook some fancy meal plan.

facts.chart: Enjoys grilling on weekends and watching football with neighbors, often with beer and snacks
facts.says: Weekends I like to grill out, watch some football with the neighbors. That's my downtime.

facts.chart: Frequent processed/cured meat intake (sausage, bacon, deli meats) several times weekly
facts.says: We go through a lot of sausage and bacon in this house, and I'll grab deli meat sandwiches sometimes too.

objectives.text: Apply the Nutrition Care Process (assessment, diagnosis, intervention, monitoring/evaluation) to synthesize anthropometric, biochemical, and dietary data into an ADIME note
Develop an accurate PES (Problem, Etiology, Signs/Symptoms) statement reflecting the link between dietary pattern and lipid abnormalities
Design evidence-based, realistic nutrition interventions tailored to shift-work schedule and food access barriers
Integrate medication adherence and side-effect concerns into nutrition counseling, including appropriate referral back to prescriber rather than independent medication advice
Use motivational interviewing techniques to explore the patient's values, readiness to change, and ambivalence about diet versus medication
Identify lifestyle and behavioral barriers (alcohol use, sedentary pattern, sleep, food cost/access) and collaboratively develop realistic, patient-centered solutions
Recognize when interprofessional referral (PCP follow-up for medication side effects, repeat labs) is indicated and communicate this to the patient without overstepping scope

scenario.studentBrief: You are a dietetics student conducting an initial telehealth nutrition assessment and counseling visit with Omar Sinclair, a 45-year-old aircraft mechanic referred by his PCP for medical nutrition therapy following a new diagnosis of dyslipidemia, prediabetes, and hypertension. Review the chart before the call. Your goals are to complete a nutrition assessment, identify a nutrition diagnosis (PES statement), and begin patient-centered counseling using motivational interviewing. Omar is pragmatic and somewhat skeptical of being told what to do - build rapport before pressing on sensitive topics like alcohol use or medication adherence.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Referral for medical nutrition therapy due to newly diagnosed dyslipidemia (elevated LDL cholesterol), with secondary diagnoses of prediabetes and hypertension.
scenario.openingLine: Hey, yeah, I'm Omar. My doctor said my cholesterol's high and sent me to talk to you. I don't really see what the big deal is, honestly, but figured I'd hear you out.
tasks: Conduct a thorough nutrition-focused history including meal pattern, food choices, beverages, alcohol use, and physical activity
Review and interpret relevant anthropometric and laboratory data (BMI, waist circumference, lipid panel, HbA1c, fasting glucose) in context of the diagnosis
Identify key barriers (medication side effects/adherence, cost/access, shift-work schedule, low health literacy) through patient-centered, non-judgmental questioning
Formulate a nutrition diagnosis (PES statement) and negotiate 1-2 realistic, specific dietary goals using motivational interviewing techniques
Document the encounter in ADIME format and identify when interprofessional referral back to the PCP is warranted

profile.setting: Telehealth video visit; patient calling from his home garage during a break, PCP referral for outpatient medical nutrition therapy
profile.summary: Omar Sinclair is a 45-year-old aircraft mechanic with new dyslipidemia (LDL 195, HDL 30, triglycerides 180), prediabetes, and hypertension, referred for medical nutrition therapy. He is pragmatic, skeptical of statins due to perceived dizziness, has low health literacy about cholesterol, and faces real barriers from shift-work scheduling, food access/cost, and undisclosed heavier alcohol intake. The case teaches learners to apply the Nutrition Care Process, build an accurate PES statement, use motivational interviewing to navigate ambivalence about diet versus medication, and recognize when to loop in the PCP about medication side effects rather than advising independently.
